en: The Philippines monitors weather within the Philippine Area of Responsibility, a boundary tracked by PAGASA to predict typhoons.
Mayon Volcano in Albay frequently erupts andesite lava, which cools to form dark, fine-grained igneous rocks.
Volcanic ash from Mount Pinatubo weathered into highly fertile andisols, helping farmers in Central Luzon grow rice.
During the habagat monsoon, warm moist air from the West Philippine Sea rises and condenses into heavy rain.
Because the equator crosses the Philippines, places like Basilan receive direct, intense sunlight year-round compared to higher latitudes.
Filipino farmers historically used the Balatik constellation, known to Western astronomers as Orion, to signal planting seasons.
Fishermen in Manila Bay rely on the gravitational pull of the moon to predict high tides for fishing.
The 1,250-kilometer Philippine Fault Zone stretches across the archipelago, causing frequent earthquakes as tectonic plates constantly shift.
The Philippines sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where the Philippine Sea Plate subducts beneath the Eurasian Plate.
El Niño warms the Pacific Ocean, causing severe dry spells that force water rationing in Metro Manila.
Surigao del Norte contains large nickel laterite deposits, which form from the weathering of iron-rich volcanic rocks.
Diwata-1, the first Philippine microsatellite, orbits Earth to capture high-resolution images of typhoons and monitor crop health.
